desc:
You have sticks with the lengths in sides. Choose any three different sticks that form a triangle of positive area and return the largest perimeter you can get. If no three sticks form such a triangle, return 0.

Three lengths x ≤ y ≤ z form a triangle of positive area exactly when x + y > z.

For example, [3, 6, 2, 3] gives 8 (sticks 3, 3, 2), because 6 is too long to pair with any two others.
hints: Only the three longest sticks of a good triple matter for its perimeter, so look at big sticks first.
Sort in descending order. For a fixed longest stick, the best partners are the next two largest ones.
Check consecutive triples (s[i], s[i+1], s[i+2]) in the sorted order; the first one with s[i+1] + s[i+2] > s[i] is the answer.
editorial: Sort the lengths in descending order. Suppose the longest stick of an optimal triangle is s[i]. The two partners that maximize the perimeter and are most likely to satisfy the inequality are s[i+1] and s[i+2], the biggest sticks still available. If even they fail (s[i+1] + s[i+2] ≤ s[i]), no pair works with s[i] as the longest side, so s[i] can be discarded.

The first index where the consecutive triple works gives the largest possible perimeter, since every triple examined before it was impossible and later ones have smaller sticks. If no index works, return 0. Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time. The failing chain grows like the Fibonacci numbers, so at most about 40 sticks can fail in a row for values below 10<sup>8</sup>.
